title: Why the Way We Pay for Healthcare Is Breaking the System — And How Paying for Value Could Fix It
summary: The United States spends more on healthcare than any nation on earth — yet ranks 37th in health outcomes. This module explains why that paradox exists, how the fee-for-service payment system created it, and how value-based care offers a fundamentally different path forward.
learningObjectives: Explain the US healthcare spending paradox using current data
Describe how fee-for-service payment works and the perverse incentives it creates
Define value-based care and distinguish it from fee-for-service
Identify the four main categories of value-based payment models
Explain why Vermont is a national leader in the shift to value-based care

children.text: Imagine paying a mechanic every time they touched your car — whether or not it ran better afterward. Now imagine that mechanic's salary depended entirely on how many parts they replaced, not on whether your car actually worked. You would quickly end up with a very expensive car that still broke down constantly. This, in essence, is how the United States pays for healthcare.

The US spent $4.5 trillion on healthcare in 2022 — roughly $13,493 per person, and 18.3 percent of the entire national economy. That is more than any other high-income country, by a wide margin. Switzerland, the second-highest spender, dedicates about 11.3 percent of its GDP to health. Germany spends 12.8 percent. Canada spends 12.2 percent.

stats.label: US Healthcare Spending (2022)
stats.context: 18.3% of GDP — the highest of any nation on earth. Source: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, 2023.

stats.label: US Health Outcomes Ranking
stats.context: Behind most peer nations in life expectancy, infant mortality, and chronic disease burden. Source: World Health Organization.

stats.label: Estimated Waste in US Healthcare
stats.context: JAMA 2019: $760B–$935B per year on unnecessary or low-value care — roughly 1 in 3 dollars spent.

children.text: And yet — despite outspending every peer nation — the US ranks 37th in overall health outcomes according to the World Health Organization. Americans live shorter lives than citizens of 40 other countries. The US infant mortality rate is nearly double that of Finland. Preventable deaths from conditions like diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease occur at far higher rates here than in comparable wealthy nations.
How Did We Get Here? Understanding Fee-for-Service

To understand why America spends so much and gets so little, you need to understand the payment system that drives almost every clinical decision made in the country. That system is called fee-for-service, often abbreviated FFS. Fee-for-service has been the dominant payment model for American medicine since the mid-20th century.

Fee-for-Service (FFS): A payment model in which healthcare providers are paid separately for each service they deliver — each office visit, each test, each procedure, each hospital day. Payment is triggered by doing something, not by whether the patient gets better.

Here is how it works in practice: a physician, hospital, or other provider submits a claim to an insurer — Medicare, Medicaid, or a private insurer — using standardized billing codes called CPT codes. Each code corresponds to a specific service: a visit, a blood draw, an MRI, a surgical procedure. The insurer reviews the claim and pays a set rate for each code. The provider's revenue depends entirely on how many services they bill, not on whether those services helped the patient.

body.analogy: Imagine a restaurant that charged you for every time a server walked past your table — whether they brought food, refilled your water, or just walked by. The restaurant's income would depend not on how satisfying your meal was, but on how many times staff interacted with you. Servers would be incentivized to walk past your table as often as possible, whether you needed anything or not.
body.bridge: In healthcare, this translates into providers ordering more tests, scheduling more follow-up visits, and performing more procedures — because each one generates revenue. Keeping a patient healthy and out of the office is financially penalized under this model.

children.text: The Perverse Incentives of Fee-for-Service

The word 'perverse' in economics means an incentive that pushes behavior in the opposite direction from what you actually want. Fee-for-service is full of perverse incentives. Consider what happens when a hospital successfully reduces readmissions by improving care coordination after discharge. Under fee-for-service, that hospital just reduced its own revenue — because each readmission generates thousands of dollars in billing.

Or consider preventive care. A primary care physician who spends an extra 30 minutes helping a diabetic patient understand diet, exercise, and medication adherence may prevent that patient from ever needing a $50,000 hospitalization. Under fee-for-service, the physician is paid a modest office visit fee for those 30 minutes. The hospital that would have done the expensive hospitalization loses revenue. The system as a whole saves money — but the individual providers doing the right thing are financially worse off.

Under fee-for-service, prevention is a cost center, not a revenue source. Providers are paid to treat illness, not to prevent it. This single fact explains more about America's healthcare crisis than almost any other.

children.text: Defining Value-Based Care: A Fundamentally Different Approach

Value-based care, sometimes called value-based payment or value-based purchasing, is a healthcare delivery and payment model in which providers are paid based on patient health outcomes rather than the volume of services provided. The key word is 'value' — defined in healthcare as the quality of care delivered divided by the cost of delivering it.

Value-Based Care: A payment and delivery model where providers earn more when they keep patients healthier, improve quality, and reduce unnecessary costs — and earn less when they deliver high volumes of low-quality or unnecessary care. The core formula: Value = Quality / Cost.

This seems like a simple idea — pay for results, not for activity. But implementing it requires solving genuinely hard problems: How do you measure quality? How do you attribute outcomes to specific providers when patients see many doctors? How do you prevent providers from avoiding sick patients to protect their quality scores? How do you account for the fact that some patients have more complex needs than others? These are the questions that value-based payment models are designed to address.

body.title: Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care at a Glance

rows.left: Do more — more visits, tests, procedures
rows.right: Keep patients healthier with fewer interventions
Provider shares in savings and losses
Clinical outcomes, population health data required

children.text: The Four Main Categories of Value-Based Payment Models

Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a family of models that shift payment from volume to value in different ways and to different degrees. Think of a spectrum: at one end is pure fee-for-service with no accountability for outcomes; at the other end is full capitation where providers take on complete financial responsibility for a population's health. Most VBC models sit somewhere in between.
Category 1: Pay-for-Performance

Pay-for-performance (P4P) is the simplest form of value-based payment. Providers still get paid fee-for-service for each service, but they receive bonuses for hitting quality targets — or face penalties for missing them. Examples include CMS's Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, which adjusts Medicare payments to hospitals based on quality scores, and the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) for physicians.
Category 2: Accountable Care Organizations and Shared Savings

Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are networks of doctors, hospitals, and other providers that work together to coordinate care for a defined group of patients. The ACO is given a benchmark spending target. If the ACO spends less than the benchmark while maintaining quality, it shares in those savings. This model keeps the fee-for-service billing infrastructure but adds accountability for total cost of care.

Medicare ACOs generated $1.87 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2022, according to CMS. As of 2024, more than 480 ACOs participate in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, covering over 11 million beneficiaries. Vermont's OneCare Vermont is an ACO that serves both Medicare and Medicaid populations — and is the centerpiece of the state's nationally recognized All-Payer Model.
Category 3: Bundled Payments

Bundled payments group all the costs for a single episode of care — say, a hip replacement surgery plus the 90 days of recovery — into one fixed payment. All providers involved must share that single payment. If they deliver great care efficiently and spend less than the bundle price, they keep the difference. If they spend more, they lose money. This directly incentivizes coordination across the care team.
Category 4: Capitation and Global Budgets

Capitation is the most fundamental shift: providers receive a fixed monthly payment per patient to cover all their care, regardless of how many services that patient uses. The provider takes on complete financial responsibility — called full risk — for the patient's health. If the patient stays healthy and uses few services, the provider keeps the surplus. Global budgets take this idea to the health-system level: an entire hospital or health system receives a fixed annual budget to care for a defined population.

body.title: How Value-Based Care Works: From Payment Design to Patient Outcome

steps.title: Define the Population
steps.description: A group of patients is attributed to a provider or health system — for example, all Medicare beneficiaries whose primary care physician is in a particular ACO.

steps.title: Set a Spending Benchmark
steps.description: Based on historical spending, a target is set for what this population's care should cost. This becomes the benchmark against which actual spending is measured.

steps.title: Measure Quality
steps.description: Quality metrics are tracked — things like diabetes control rates, readmission rates, preventive screening completion, and patient experience scores.

steps.title: Deliver Care with Accountability
steps.description: Providers deliver care as they normally would, but now have financial incentive to coordinate, prevent, and reduce unnecessary services.

steps.title: Reconcile and Share Savings
steps.description: At year end, actual spending is compared to the benchmark. If the provider spent less while maintaining quality, they share in the savings. If they spent more, they may face a penalty.

children.text: Vermont: A National Laboratory for Value-Based Care

Vermont is the only state in the nation operating an approved All-Payer Accountable Care Organization Model — a program that brings Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance under a single set of quality and spending targets for the first time in American history. This makes Vermont uniquely important to anyone studying value-based care. What Vermont learns, the nation watches.

The Vermont All-Payer ACO Model was approved by CMS in 2016 and launched in January 2017. At its center is OneCare Vermont, a statewide ACO that contracts with hospitals, physicians, and community organizations across the state. OneCare Vermont currently serves approximately 240,000 Vermonters — nearly 40 percent of the state's population — through its attributed beneficiary program.

body.title: OneCare Vermont: Vermont's Statewide ACO
body.body: OneCare Vermont launched in 2017 as the operational vehicle for Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model. It serves Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance members under a unified set of quality metrics and spending targets. The organization works with 119 primary care practices, 14 hospitals, and hundreds of community providers across the state to coordinate care for approximately 240,000 attributed Vermonters. Unlike a traditional insurer, OneCare Vermont does not manage claims — instead, it manages the health of a population, investing in care coordination, social services navigation, and community health workers.
body.outcome: In performance years where OneCare met quality targets, Vermont demonstrated lower-than-expected spending growth — a meaningful achievement given Vermont's older, sicker-than-average, and largely rural population.
body.source: Vermont Agency of Administration / CMS All-Payer Model Performance Reports, 2017–2024

children.text: The Green Mountain Care Board

Vermont's All-Payer Model is overseen by the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB), a state agency with broad authority to regulate healthcare costs, review hospital budgets, and set statewide health spending targets. The GMCB is one of the most powerful state-level healthcare cost-control bodies in the nation. It reviews and approves hospital budgets every year — meaning hospitals cannot simply raise prices without regulatory approval.

This combination — a statewide ACO (OneCare Vermont) operating under regulatory oversight (GMCB), with a federal partnership (CMS All-Payer Model) — makes Vermont's healthcare system genuinely unique. Understanding how it works, and why it was designed this way, is one of the most valuable things you can learn if you work in Vermont healthcare.

body.title: Medicare Shared Savings Program: The Largest VBC Program in the World
body.body: The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), created by the Affordable Care Act in 2012 and operated by CMS, is the largest ACO program in the world. Participating ACOs take responsibility for the total cost and quality of care for their attributed Medicare beneficiaries. ACOs that spend below their benchmark while meeting quality standards share a portion of savings with Medicare. Those in higher-risk tracks may also face penalties for overspending.
body.outcome: In 2022, Medicare ACOs generated $1.87 billion in net savings for Medicare while serving 11 million beneficiaries. ACOs in higher-risk tracks consistently outperformed lower-risk tracks, demonstrating that meaningful financial accountability improves performance.
body.source: CMS Medicare Shared Savings Program 2022 Performance Year Results, published 2023

children.text: Why This Matters to You, Wherever You Work

If you are a nurse, this transformation changes what your work looks like. Value-based care prioritizes care coordination, discharge planning, chronic disease management, and patient education — all activities that nurses are uniquely positioned to lead. Under fee-for-service, a nurse who prevented a readmission by spending extra time on discharge education was not generating revenue. Under VBC, that same nurse is helping the organization succeed financially.

If you are a hospital administrator, VBC means thinking differently about your budget. Revenue is no longer simply a function of volume. Quality scores, total cost of care for your population, and care coordination infrastructure become central financial drivers. Understanding which patients are at highest risk of expensive preventable events — and investing in keeping them well — becomes essential to financial sustainability.

body.analogy: Transitioning from fee-for-service to value-based care is like converting a city from individual car ownership to a public transit system while everyone is still driving to work. You cannot shut down all the roads at once — you have to build the trains while traffic is still running, convince people the new system is better, and gradually shift incentives until the old system is obsolete.
body.bridge: In healthcare, providers must continue billing fee-for-service while simultaneously building the care coordination, data, and team infrastructure that VBC requires. Organizations that invest in both simultaneously face real financial strain during the transition period — but those that do not invest will be left behind.

body.misconception: Value-based care means providers just get paid less for doing the same work.
body.reality: VBC redistributes financial incentives — it does not simply cut payments. Providers who deliver high-quality, efficient, well-coordinated care can earn significantly more under VBC than under fee-for-service. The providers who lose money are those who were generating revenue through high volumes of low-value care.

body.misconception: Value-based care is a cost-cutting measure that will hurt patients by rationing necessary care.
body.reality: The evidence shows the opposite: VBC programs consistently improve quality scores, reduce preventable hospitalizations, and increase preventive care rates. The goal is to eliminate waste and low-value care — not necessary care. Patients in high-performing ACOs receive more preventive services, not fewer essential treatments.

children.text: What You Will Learn in This Course

This course has six modules, each building on the last. Module 2 dives into the economics: how money flows through the healthcare system and the mechanics of each major payment model in depth. Module 3 focuses on clinical practice: how VBC changes the daily reality of delivering care. Module 4 examines the policy landscape: the federal programs and Vermont-specific structures that govern the transition. Module 5 covers technology: the data infrastructure that makes VBC possible. Module 6 addresses the most urgent challenge: health equity, and how VBC can be designed to reduce — rather than worsen — the disparities that exist in every healthcare system.

By the end of this course, you will have a sophisticated understanding of one of the most consequential transformations happening in American healthcare. You will understand not just what value-based care is, but why it was designed the way it is, how it plays out in real clinical settings, and what it means for patients, providers, and communities across Vermont and the nation.

The question is no longer whether healthcare should move to value-based payment — it is how fast and how completely. Every major payer, every major health system, and every serious policymaker now agrees that fee-for-service as the dominant payment model is unsustainable. The only debate is about the pace and mechanics of transition.

body.question: A hospital reduces readmissions by 15% through an improved discharge education program. Under fee-for-service, what happens to the hospital's revenue? Under a value-based ACO model, what happens?
body.hint: Think about what generates revenue under each model.
body.answer: Under fee-for-service, the hospital's revenue decreases — each avoided readmission represents a lost billing opportunity worth thousands of dollars. Under a value-based ACO model, the hospital's financial performance improves — lower spending relative to the benchmark means a larger share of savings, and better quality scores protect or increase future payment rates. This contrast illustrates the core difference between the two systems: FFS rewards volume, VBC rewards outcomes.

body.question: What makes Vermont's healthcare system unique compared to every other state in the country?
body.hint: Think about the payer mix and the role of OneCare Vermont.
body.answer: Vermont is the only state operating an approved All-Payer ACO Model — meaning Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance all operate under a single set of unified quality and spending targets. In every other state, these payers operate independently with different rules, creating fragmentation that makes coordinated care harder. Vermont's model, anchored by OneCare Vermont and overseen by the Green Mountain Care Board, attempts to align all payers behind shared goals for the first time in American history.

body.title: Key Takeaways: Module 1
points: The US spends $4.5 trillion on healthcare (18.3% of GDP) — more than any nation — yet ranks 37th in health outcomes, a paradox driven largely by fee-for-service payment incentives.

Fee-for-service pays providers per service delivered, creating perverse incentives to do more regardless of whether it helps patients. Prevention, coordination, and efficiency are financially penalized.
Value-based care is a family of payment models that pay for outcomes rather than volume — aligning provider incentives with patient health. The core formula: Value = Quality / Cost.
The four main VBC model categories are pay-for-performance, shared savings ACOs, bundled payments, and capitation/global budgets — each shifting more financial risk and accountability to providers.

Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model — the only one of its kind in the US — makes Vermont a national laboratory for value-based care transformation, with OneCare Vermont serving approximately 240,000 Vermonters.
The transition from FFS to VBC requires changes in payment contracts, data infrastructure, clinical workflows, and organizational culture — and is a multi-decade journey, not a single event.
